questions.question: In unidirectional data flow between a ViewModel and a screen, which description is correct?
options: State flows down from the ViewModel to the UI, and events flow up from the UI to the ViewModel
The UI and ViewModel share one mutable object and both write to it (two-way binding)
The UI owns the state and pushes a full copy of it to the ViewModel after every change the user makes on screen
Events flow down from the ViewModel to the UI, and state flows up from the UI
questions.explanation: In UDF the ViewModel is the single source of truth: it exposes state that the UI only renders, and the UI reports user actions back by calling ViewModel functions. Two-way binding lets both sides write the same data, which is exactly what UDF avoids.

questions.question: If a ViewModel exposes a public `MutableStateFlow<UiState>`, the ViewModel is still the only place where the screen's state can change.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A public `MutableStateFlow` lets any caller, including the UI, assign `value`, so the ViewModel is no longer the single source of truth. Keep `private val _state = MutableStateFlow(...)` and expose `val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state.asStateFlow()`.

questions.question: What does this MVI-style reducer program print?
options: 0 4 [add2, add3, add4]
4 4 [add2, add3, add4]
0 9 [add2, add3, add4]
questions.explanation: The reducer never mutates: each step returns a new `State` via `copy`, so `start` stays at 0. `Reset` only zeroes `count` and keeps `log`, so the result is 2+3 → 0 → 4 with all three log entries.

questions.question: A composable screen needs to render `viewModel.uiState: StateFlow<UiState>`. What is the recommended way to read it?
options: `val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`
`val state by viewModel.uiState.observeAsState()`
`val state = viewModel.uiState.value`
`LaunchedEffect(Unit) { viewModel.uiState.collect { cached = it } }` with a plain `var cached`
questions.explanation: `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` turns the flow into Compose state and stops collecting when the lifecycle drops below STARTED. Reading `.value` directly doesn't subscribe, so the screen won't update, and `observeAsState()` is for LiveData.

questions.question: Which of these should a ViewModel NOT keep a reference to? Select all that apply.
options: A `TextView` from the screen's layout
The `Activity`, used as a `Context`
The `NavController`
A `SavedStateHandle`
A repository interface injected by Hilt
questions.explanation: A ViewModel outlives configuration changes, so holding Views, an Activity or a NavController leaks the old screen and couples the ViewModel to UI objects. The ViewModel should expose state or a navigation request that the UI acts on. `SavedStateHandle` and injected repositories are normal ViewModel dependencies.

questions.question: A feed screen must keep showing the current list while pull-to-refresh runs, and show a transient error message on top of the list if the refresh fails. Which UiState model fits best?
options: `data class FeedUiState(val items: List<Item>, val isRefreshing: Boolean, val userMessage: String?)`
`sealed interface FeedUiState { Loading; Success(items); Error(message) }`
Three separate `StateFlow`s (`items`, `isRefreshing`, `error`) exposed from the ViewModel, which the composable combines into what it shows
A `MutableList<Item>` exposed from the ViewModel and mutated in place on refresh
questions.explanation: Here loading, content and error can legitimately coexist, so one data class with independent fields fits. A sealed `Loading/Success/Error` would throw away the list when switching to `Loading`. Separate flows push the combining logic into the UI, and a mutable list breaks immutability.

questions.question: In classic MVP, the Presenter holds a reference to the View interface, so it must be attached and detached with the lifecycle to avoid leaks and calls into a destroyed screen.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The MVP Presenter calls `view.showItems(...)` directly, so it must drop the reference in `onDestroy` and gets nothing back across rotation unless you add your own retention. MVVM avoids this: the ViewModel has no view reference and the UI observes its state.

questions.question: Compared with `data class UiState(val isLoading: Boolean, val data: Data?, val error: String?)`, what does a `sealed interface UiState { Loading; Success(data); Error(message) }` give you? Select all that apply.
options: Combinations like loading with an error at the same time can't be represented
A `when (state)` without `else` is exhaustive, so the compiler flags a missing branch
It's the easiest way to keep the old data on screen while a refresh runs
You can change one field with `copy` and leave the others untouched
questions.explanation: Each subtype carries only the data valid for that state, so impossible states disappear and `when` is exhaustive. Keeping old data during a refresh, and updating single fields with `copy`, are what the flat data class is good at.

questions.question: Why is `_state.update { it.copy(query = q) }` preferred over `_state.value = _state.value.copy(query = q)`?
options: `update` retries with compare-and-set, so two concurrent updates can't silently overwrite each other
`update` forces every collector to be notified, even when the new state is equal to the old one, so the UI always redraws
Assigning `value` directly only works on the main thread
`update` saves the new state into `SavedStateHandle` automatically
questions.explanation: The read-then-assign version is not atomic: if another coroutine updates the state between the read and the write, its change is lost. `update` loops on `compareAndSet` until its transformation is applied to the latest value. Neither form notifies collectors about an equal value, and `value` can be set from any thread.

questions.question: A reusable `ExpandableSearchBar` composable needs to track whether it is expanded and which suggestion is highlighted. Two of them can appear on the same screen. Where should this state live?
options: In a plain state holder class created with a `rememberSearchBarState()` function, like `LazyListState`
In a dedicated `SearchBarViewModel`, obtained with `viewModel()` inside the component itself so the state survives configuration changes
In the screen's ViewModel, as two fields per search bar
In top-level global `mutableStateOf` variables
questions.explanation: This is UI element state with no business logic, so a component-level plain state holder remembered in composition fits. ViewModels are screen-level: `viewModel()` without a key returns the same instance for the same owner, so both bars would share one state. Global variables are shared by every instance too.

questions.question: A ViewModel starts loading in `init { viewModelScope.launch { ... } }` and exposes `StateFlow<UiState>`. The user rotates the phone while the request is in flight. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The coroutine keeps running, because the ViewModel isn't cleared on a configuration change
The recreated screen gets the current state (e.g. `Loading`) as soon as it collects, then `Success` when the load finishes
`init` runs again for the new Activity, so a second request starts
The result is lost, because the old screen's collector was cancelled while the request was running
questions.explanation: The same ViewModel instance is handed to the new Activity, so `init` doesn't run again and `viewModelScope` keeps working. A `StateFlow` always holds its latest value, so the new collector gets it right away. Only the collector was cancelled, not the work that writes the state.

questions.question: In MVI, the reducer `(State, Action) -> State` should be a pure function, and work such as network calls or navigation is handled outside it as a side effect.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A pure reducer always gives the same new state for the same inputs, which makes it easy to test and reason about. Side effects such as API calls run elsewhere and dispatch new actions with their results, and one-off effects such as navigation go through a separate effects stream.

questions.question: A profile screen needs `userRepo.user: Flow<User>` and `settingsRepo.settings: Flow<Settings>`, and must update whenever either changes. What is the idiomatic way to build the ViewModel's UI state?
options: `combine(user, settings) { u, s -> ProfileUiState(u, s) }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProfileUiState())`
`user.zip(settings) { u, s -> ProfileUiState(u, s) }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = ProfileUiState())
Expose both flows and let the composable merge them into one state
`user.flatMapLatest { settings }` and build the state from the settings value alone
questions.explanation: `combine` emits a new value whenever either source emits, using the latest from each, and `stateIn` turns the result into a `StateFlow` scoped to the ViewModel. `zip` pairs emissions one-to-one, so a settings change wouldn't show until the user flow also emits. Merging in the composable puts state logic in the UI.

questions.question: After a failed save, the screen must show a snackbar once. What does the Android architecture guidance recommend?
options: Put `userMessage: String?` in the UiState, show it from the UI, then call `viewModel.userMessageShown()` to clear it
Pass the `SnackbarHostState` to the ViewModel and call `showSnackbar` from there
Emit the message on a `MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1)` so that a collector that subscribes late, for example after a rotation, still receives it
Show a `Toast` from the ViewModel using the Activity context
questions.explanation: Modelling the message as state that the UI acknowledges means it survives rotation and is shown exactly once. Giving UI objects to the ViewModel leaks them and breaks UDF. A `replay = 1` SharedFlow replays the old message to every new collector, so the snackbar shows again after rotation.

questions.question: On a sign-up form, which of these belong in the ViewModel rather than in the composable? Select all that apply.
options: Deciding whether Submit is enabled based on the validation rules
Calling the repository to create the account
Turning a repository failure into the message the screen shows
The current scroll position of the form's `LazyColumn`
The progress of the button's press animation
questions.explanation: Validation rules, data calls and error mapping are business or screen logic. Kept in the ViewModel, they can be tested without UI and they survive configuration changes. Scroll position and animation progress are UI element state, which belongs in the composition (`rememberLazyListState`, animation APIs).

questions.question: This local JVM unit test crashes with an `IllegalStateException` about the Main dispatcher. Why, and what is the usual fix?
options: `viewModelScope` needs `Dispatchers.Main`, which plain JVM tests lack; replace it via `Dispatchers.setMain(...)` in a test rule
ViewModels can only be constructed inside instrumented tests on a device or emulator, so the test has to move to `androidTest`
`runTest` can't read `StateFlow.value`, so the assertion must use `first()`
`FakeTasksRepository` must be replaced by a real Room database
questions.explanation: `viewModelScope` runs on `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`, which needs Android's main looper. Replacing it with a `TestDispatcher` via `Dispatchers.setMain` makes the ViewModel testable on the JVM with a fake repository, and you then assert the states it emits. ViewModels are plain classes and don't need an instrumented test.

questions.question: What does this reducer print?
questions.code:
sealed interface State
data object Idle : State
data object Loading : State
data class Loaded(val n: Int) : State

sealed interface Action
data object Fetch : Action
data class Done(val n: Int) : Action

fun reduce(s: State, a: Action): State = when (a) {
    Fetch -> if (s is Loading) s else Loading
    is Done -> if (s is Loading) Loaded(a.n) else s
}

fun main() {
    val start: State = Idle
    val actions = listOf(Done(1), Fetch, Fetch, Done(2), Done(3))
    println(actions.runningFold(start, ::reduce).joinToString(" -> "))
}
options: Idle -> Idle -> Loading -> Loading -> Loaded(n=2) -> Loaded(n=2)
Idle -> Idle -> Loading -> Loading -> Loaded(n=2) -> Loaded(n=3)
Idle -> Loaded(n=1) -> Loading -> Loading -> Loaded(n=2) -> Loaded(n=3)
Idle -> Loading -> Loading -> Loaded(n=2) -> Loaded(n=2)
questions.explanation: `runningFold` includes the initial value, then one state per action. `Done` is only accepted while `Loading`, so `Done(1)` in `Idle` and `Done(3)` in `Loaded` are ignored, and a second `Fetch` while loading changes nothing. Ignoring actions that make no sense in the current state is how a reducer prevents impossible transitions.

questions.question: The first `load()` fails with message "Timeout". The user taps Retry and the second call returns 3 items. The UI shows an error banner when `error != null` and the list otherwise below it. What does the user see?
options: The 3 items, with the stale "Timeout" banner still showing
Only the 3 items
Only the "Timeout" error banner, with no items
A spinner that never goes away, since `isLoading` is never reset
questions.explanation: `copy` keeps every field you don't mention, and no step ever clears `error`, so the final state is `isLoading=false, items=[3 items], error="Timeout"`. Each transition must reset the fields it invalidates (e.g. `error = null` when loading starts), or the state should be modelled as a sealed type where this combination can't exist.

questions.question: If a ViewModel sets `_state.value = UiState(count = 1)` while the current value is already an equal `UiState(count = 1)` (a data class), collectors receive the new value again.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `StateFlow` is conflated by equality: assigning a value `==` to the current one is a no-op, and data classes compare structurally. So you can't re-trigger the UI by re-sending an equal state, which is one reason one-off events shouldn't be modelled as "set the same state again".

questions.question: An MVI ViewModel sends one-off effects (e.g. `NavigateToDetails`) through `Channel<Effect>(Channel.BUFFERED).receiveAsFlow()` rather than a `MutableSharedFlow<Effect>()` with no replay. What is the main reason?
options: The channel buffers an effect until a collector receives it, while a SharedFlow with no subscribers drops it (e.g. during a rotation)
A channel delivers every effect to all of its collectors at the same time, whereas a SharedFlow hands each one to a single collector only
A channel replays the last effect to each new collector, so it's never missed
A SharedFlow can't be collected from a composable
questions.explanation: Effects aren't state, so they're kept out of the reducer's state and sent on a separate stream. With `replay = 0`, a SharedFlow emission with no active collector is lost, but a buffered channel holds it until the new screen collects it. Each channel element goes to exactly one receiver, and channels don't replay.
